headline: NZ Parliament Advances Disability Support Bill Amid Disputes Over Welfare and Winter Payments
summary: An extended sitting carried Parliament’s business into Thursday, where MPs completed committee consideration of the Disability Support Services Bill and began debating proposed welfare eligibility changes. The debates exposed sharp disagreements over disability rights, support for young jobseekers and pensioners, and the Government’s economic and infrastructure priorities, against a backdrop of election-year political tension.

topicSummaries.topic: Disability Support Services Bill Clears Committee Without Amendment
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The bill sets a legal framework for disability support services and could affect how future funding and service decisions are made.
topicSummaries.content: The House considered the Disability Support Services Bill in committee during the extended sitting and agreed to its parts and schedules, rejecting Opposition amendments; the bill was reported without amendment, rather than finally passed by Parliament. Disability Issues Minister Louise Upston said it would clarify the system without changing current eligibility or support, and said future support programmes would be developed with consultation. Labour and Green MPs argued the bill largely codifies existing arrangements, leaves significant detail to secondary legislation and does not provide enough safeguards on family contributions, means testing or consultation. The debate is set to continue through the bill’s remaining stages.

keyExchanges.speaker: Hon Louise Upston (National)
keyExchanges.quote: I will say it again: the bill does not change eligibility, entitlement, or support that people receive.

keyExchanges.speaker: Hon Priyanca Radhakrishnan (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: all this bill does is codify a system that is fragmented and not working for disabled people and carers.

topicSummaries.topic: Welfare Bill Would Add Parental Test for Some 18- and 19-Year-Olds
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The proposed test could affect whether young adults can receive Jobseeker Support, while a separate change would tighten access to the Accommodation Supplement for some homeowners.
topicSummaries.content: Social Development and Employment Minister Louise Upston began the second-reading debate on the Social Security (Jobseeker Support and Accommodation Supplement) Amendment Bill. The proposal would require some 18- and 19-year-olds to show they cannot reasonably rely on parental financial support before receiving Jobseeker Support or the equivalent emergency benefit; it would also raise the accommodation-cost threshold for some homeowners seeking the supplement. Upston said the changes were intended to target assistance and encourage young people into work, education or training, while retaining support where parents cannot provide it. Labour and Green MPs argued the measure could deepen hardship and make young people more dependent on family support; the second-reading debate was interrupted and remained unfinished.

keyExchanges.speaker: Hon Louise Upston (National)
keyExchanges.quote: when individuals or their parents are able to provide that support, our expectation is that they should do so, not other taxpayers.

keyExchanges.speaker: Hon Willow-Jean Prime (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: In terms of impact on young people and their families, the costs will significantly outweigh the benefits.

topicSummaries.topic: Urgent Debate on Winter Energy Payments Declined
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The dispute concerns winter payments that Labour said had stopped for 15,000 pensioners and veterans, potentially affecting their ability to meet heating costs.
topicSummaries.content: The Speaker declined an urgent debate sought by Green MP Ricardo Menéndez March over reports that people had lost winter energy payments, saying legislation would provide an appropriate opportunity to discuss the issue. Labour MPs challenged that reasoning, saying the Government had not committed to amending the law or provided a timetable. In the General Debate, Opposition MPs criticised the Government’s handling of the issue and described the impact on affected older people; the transcript records no firm timetable for a legislative fix.

keyExchanges.speaker: Speaker
keyExchanges.quote: That will provide the appropriate opportunity to debate it.

keyExchanges.speaker: Hon Willow-Jean Prime (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: She has not given a time frame for that, and it will potentially be in the next parliamentary term, so we won’t have the ability to debate this when the legislation comes to the House, because she hasn’t committed to that.

topicSummaries.topic: Nursing Workforce Figures Spark Dispute Over 54 FTE Increase
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: Staffing levels in public hospitals affect patients’ access to care and the capacity to provide treatments on time.
topicSummaries.content: Labour health spokesperson Ayesha Verrall asked whether Health New Zealand’s nursing workforce had increased by a net 54 full-time equivalents between the quarters ending March 2024 and March 2026. Health Minister Simeon Brown initially cited a different period, saying the workforce had grown by 1,640 FTE since September 2023, and pointed to vacancies and recruitment activity. After repeated questions and Speaker intervention, Brown confirmed the 54 FTE figure for the period in the original question. The parties continued to dispute how to interpret the figures and whether recruitment had been constrained by a hiring freeze.

keyExchanges.speaker: Hon Dr Ayesha Verrall (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: Is the answer to my primary question “54”?

keyExchanges.speaker: Hon Simeon Brown (National)
keyExchanges.quote: Yes.

topicSummaries.topic: Investment Boost’s $6.6B Tax Relief Becomes Election-Economy Flashpoint
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The policy changes business tax bills, while the debate over its effects touches on investment, wages, jobs and the Government’s revenue choices.
topicSummaries.content: Finance Minister Nicola Willis defended Investment Boost, which lets businesses deduct an additional 20 percent of the cost of eligible new assets, saying it is intended to encourage investment and productivity. Willis said the policy is forecast to reduce business taxes by $6.6 billion over four years and argued that removing it would increase taxes on firms. Labour MPs questioned how many businesses had claimed the deduction and how many jobs could be attributed to it; Willis said final tax-return data was not yet available to establish the number of claims or isolate the policy’s employment effects. The issue featured prominently in partisan exchanges over proposed taxes and the Government’s economic record.

keyExchanges.speaker: Hon Barbara Edmonds (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: How many actual jobs are attributed to Investment Boost in the last year?

keyExchanges.speaker: Hon Nicola Willis (National)
keyExchanges.quote: we do not yet have the data about how many people claimed Investment Boost in the year previous.

topicSummaries.topic: Regional Council Elections Set to End Under Local Government Reform Plan
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The reform could change how regional decisions are made and how directly residents elect representatives responsible for local services and planning.
topicSummaries.content: In the Estimates debate, Local Government Minister Simon Watts confirmed that regional council elections would not take place in 2028, with regional functions expected to move into new amalgamated unitary councils. He said the Government would provide further details as its reform process progressed, including work on voluntary “Head Start” proposals and a later backstop process. Labour and Green MPs questioned what governance arrangements would replace elected regional councils, how communities would be consulted and whether councils would face significant transition costs. Watts said proposals and possible support for transition costs were still under consideration.

keyExchanges.speaker: Lemauga Lydia Sosene (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: Regional councillors will not be elected in 2028. What sits in their place?

keyExchanges.speaker: Hon Simon Watts (National)
keyExchanges.quote: In effect, the functions of regional council will form part of new amalgamated unitary councils across the country

topicSummaries.topic: Transport Funding Gap Leaves Planned Fuel Tax Rise Unresolved
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: Decisions on fuel taxes and transport funding could affect motorists, public transport investment and the timing of road and maintenance projects.
topicSummaries.content: During the Transport Estimates debate, Labour MP Tracey McLellan questioned how the National Land Transport Fund would meet its costs beyond 2027-28, noting its reliance on borrowing and uncertainty around planned fuel excise and road-user-charge increases. Transport Minister Chris Bishop acknowledged a funding challenge and said the Government had not decided whether scheduled increases from January 2027 would proceed, although he considered them unlikely. He also said the next Government Policy Statement on land transport would be consulted on before July 2027, while an interim ministerial statement gave councils guidance but had no legal status. MPs also raised concerns about maintenance, local roads and the sequencing of major projects.

keyExchanges.speaker: Dr Tracey McLellan (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: The National Land Transport Fund is, essentially, a Budget risk because it doesn’t have sufficient funding beyond 2027-28 to cover what are its ongoing activities and debt.

keyExchanges.speaker: Hon Chris Bishop (National)
keyExchanges.quote: We see it as unlikely, but we haven’t made a decision yet, and so, when we do, we will let you know.

topicSummaries.topic: Tertiary Fee Increases Challenged Amid Student Hardship Concerns
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: Higher fees may add to the cost of study for students already facing financial pressure, while funding decisions affect the future capacity of tertiary providers.
topicSummaries.content: In the Tertiary Education Estimates debate, Labour MPs questioned the Government’s decision to allow another 6 percent increase in student fees and raised concerns about student hardship and reduced Fees Free funding. Minister Penny Simmonds said the permitted fee increase aligned fees with cumulative inflation over the period discussed and helped providers manage cost pressures. She said student allowances had risen with inflation and hardship grants remained available, while describing universities as financially strong and saying support remained for polytechnics. MPs also queried funding for polytechnic transitions and pathways for young people not in education, employment or training.

keyExchanges.speaker: Shanan Halbert (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: why was the decision made to allow tertiary institutions to increase their fees by yet another 6 percent?

keyExchanges.speaker: Hon Penny Simmonds (National)
keyExchanges.quote: the 6 percent increase, or the ability to increase fees by 6 percent again, ensured that for that period from 2018 to 2026, the fee increases were roughly aligned with what the cumulative inflation was over that period.

topicSummaries.topic: Luxon Faces Opposition Questions Over National Leadership Challenge
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: Questions about leadership and ministerial confidence can shape perceptions of government stability and distract from policy issues affecting the public.
topicSummaries.content: Opposition leader Chris Hipkins pressed Prime Minister Christopher Luxon on when he learned of an internal challenge and whether other ministers had urged him to stand down. The Speaker ruled that some questions about party caucus matters were not admissible, while allowing questions connected to Luxon’s actions as Prime Minister and the sacking of Chris Penk. Luxon said Penk was the only person to challenge for the leadership and dismissed the Opposition’s focus as petty; the issue also featured prominently in the General Debate, with Labour alleging turmoil and Government MPs accusing the Opposition of focusing on personalities and taxes.

keyExchanges.speaker: Rt Hon Chris Hipkins (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: Did any other Minister in his Government indicate that he should stand down as Prime Minister during the last two weeks; if so, why didn’t he sack them too?

keyExchanges.speaker: Rt Hon Christopher Luxon (National)
keyExchanges.quote: As has been reported, Chris Penk was the only person to challenge for the leadership; he was working for himself.

topicSummaries.topic: Prime Minister Says Current Data Centre Growth Should Not Lift Power Prices
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: Large data centres require substantial electricity, raising questions about future power costs for households and businesses.
topicSummaries.content: Green co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick questioned whether the Government had assessed the electricity-price effects of hyperscale data centres, including a proposed 280-megawatt Southland facility. Luxon said the Government supported data centres and argued that some projects were backed by investment in additional generation. After Swarbrick said he had not directly answered whether advice had been sought, Luxon cited Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment advice that expected data-centre growth should not put upward pressure on electricity prices. He also said the Government intended to develop common rules, including expectations around additional generation.

keyExchanges.speaker: Chlöe Swarbrick (Green)
keyExchanges.quote: So can he guarantee that the 280 megawatt Southland data centre will not push up electricity prices for households and businesses?

keyExchanges.speaker: Rt Hon Christopher Luxon (National)
keyExchanges.quote: The Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment advises that if current data centre growth continues as expected, there should be no upward pressure on electricity prices.

conclusion: The sitting advanced major disability and welfare legislation while leaving unresolved disputes over public support, household costs and how the Government will fund and deliver essential services.
